extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy (readers studying Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: An introductory commentary summarizing Aristotle's central ethical standards and concepts (happiness, moral virtue, doctrine of the mean, habituation, practical wisdom, justice, pleasure, friendship) and their role in moral and political life. Useful for readers seeking the principal evaluative criteria in Aristotle's Ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of Ethics: practical end and knowledge aimed at the good
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of the enquiry is the acquisition and propagation of a certain kind of knowledge (science) subsidiary to a practical end: knowledge of what is best for man and of the conditions of its realisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical knowledge is not merely theoretical; it is oriented to action and the organisation of human life. Treatises should aim to supply rules that serve practical life rather than mathematical precision. The introduction stresses that such knowledge is deficient in exactness and must be tested by experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of practical/moral rules: generality and allowance for exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical or moral rules are only general and always admit of exceptions; at their very best practical rules state probabilities, not certainties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect 'a mathematics of conduct'—rules guide by indicating probable rightness in recurring situations. Authors or practitioners should recognise limits of universalizing moral precepts and rely on experience to apply rules contextually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Happiness (eudaimonia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human Happiness lies in activity or energising, that in a way peculiar to man: the activity not of reason alone but of a being who possesses reason and applies it; it presupposes development of certain relevant powers and capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness is the supreme end; evaluations of life or conduct should ask whether actions cultivate the powers (virtues) that enable this distinctive rational activity. Physical pleasures, wealth, power, or mere possessions are rejected as constituting happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtues as acquired states formed by habituation
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral virtues are not mere moods, feelings, or natural endowments but permanent states of the agent produced by habituation—the repeated doing of acts—which fix aptitudes in one direction by discipline and imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of character should focus on stable dispositions formed by practice. Formation of good character requires directed discipline and social guidance; mere intellectual instruction is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of the Mean (rightness as the mean)
rubrics_metrics.description: Right action or feeling is an adaptation or adjustment to the special requirements of a situation—doing or feeling just the amount required, neither more nor less; wrongdoing is excess or defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'mean' as a heuristic for identifying virtues and their corresponding vices (excess and defect). Application is situation-dependent; rules can be given, but the exactly right amount must often be determined by practical intuition in the moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral action requires knowledge and acceptance of the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral virtue prescribes obedience to a rule of conduct accepted by the agent as valid for a class of recurrent situations; such obedience requires knowledge of the rule and acceptance of it as the agent's guiding rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between mere external conformity and internal acceptance. Evaluations should check whether the agent understands and endorses the rule as their own standard, though not necessarily able to state its theoretical ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility: voluntariness, coercion, ignorance, and deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Coercion and ignorance of relevant circumstances render acts involuntary and exempt the doer from responsibility; voluntary acts imply responsibility. Deliberate acts imply choice (deliberation) and are especially revealing of the agent's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging actions, consider whether they were voluntary, the presence of ignorance or coercion, and whether the act was the result of deliberation. Inner consent and choice increase responsibility; neither passion nor ignorance of the right rule necessarily extenuates responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as a moral virtue for citizens (distributive and corrective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice, in a restricted civic sense, is the special goodness of character required of adult citizens for administering civic functions. Distributive justice concerns allocation of gains or shares (in a limited, not political-power sense), while corrective justice concerns legal redress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'justice' in context: here it is practical fairmindedness for civic duties (judging, administering) rather than high-level legislating. Attempts to give precise mathematical forms to justice principles are treated cautiously; evaluate on practical fit to civic roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodness of intellect: theoretical vs practical wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Goodness of intellect has two supreme forms—Theoretical Wisdom (apprehends eternal laws, not directly about conduct) and Practical Wisdom (the master science of human life that supplies right rules of conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical wisdom depends on and presupposes moral virtue; it is the capacity to produce and justify right rules for action. In assessing judgment or policy, evaluate whether practical wisdom is present (ability to see ends and deduce fitting means) and whether it is grounded in developed character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of moral virtue and practical wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: True practical wisdom and true goodness of character are interdependent; neither is genuinely possible or 'completely' present without the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating agents or actions, check for both intellectual understanding and habituated moral disposition; the absence of one often produces 'cleverness' or unscrupulous practical success rather than genuine virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incontinence (akrasia): knowledge can fail to produce right action
rubrics_metrics.description: An agent may know what is right and yet chronically fail to act accordingly; weakness of will (incontinence) occurs when desire overpowers deliberation—even though the agent's will may be divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume knowledge suffices for moral conduct. Analyses of behavior should account for the rational elements in desire and the situational forces that lead to repeated failure despite knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as integral complement to ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship (Books VIII–IX) is a necessary and attractive complement to the account of Greek morality, containing profound reflections on the metaphysics of friendship or love and enriching the ethical picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of the good life and moral education should include social bonds and friendships as essential components; they help complete the moral theory beyond abstract rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure's role: concomitant and index of perfect activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is the natural concomitant and index of perfect activity—distinguishable but inseparable from it. Pleasure is always a good in itself, but its value depends on the worth of the activity with which it is conjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating pursuits or policies, distinguish mere pleasures from pleasures that accompany high-grade activities; the latter enhance the good life, but pleasure alone does not constitute the best life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest good: contemplative life as supreme happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest and most satisfying form of life is the contemplative life—the life of the philosopher, dedicated to scientific and philosophic contemplation—because it is the life of the highest activity of the intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In normative evaluation, rank forms of life by the kind and excellence of activity they enable; recognise that the contemplative ideal may be limited in accessibility and that the practical life remains important for most people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the State and Law in moral formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The production of good character is largely achieved by the Political Community or State, whose main instrument is Law; the State serves as an educative agency giving individuals opportunities for self-development and appreciation of new goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and institutional design should be judged by their capacity to cultivate virtuous dispositions and enable the conditions (education, laws, institutions) for citizens to achieve the good life.
